findings.title: No code produces Table 1, Figure 2 or Figure 4 (tabular experiments)
findings.quote:
## Project Structure

```
recalx_clean/
├── recalx/
│   ├── __init__.py          # Main exports
│   ├── calibration.py       # Temperature scaling and calibration metrics
│   ├── perturbations.py     # Feature perturbation utilities
│   ├── model.py             # Simple MLP for tabular demos
│   └── image_wrapper.py     # ImageNet model wrapper
├── data/                    # Demo data and precomputed temperatures
├── demo_tabular.ipynb       # Tabular demo (Electricity dataset)
├── demo_images.ipynb        # Image demo (DenseNet121 on ImageNet)
└── requirements.txt
```
findings.claim: The README's complete file listing is four library modules plus two demo notebooks. A repository-wide search (check_repo_coverage.py) finds no occurrence of Covertype, Credit, regression, bootstrap/confidence interval, or any result script ('Pol' matches only inside embedded base64 image data in the notebooks); the only tabular pipeline is demo_tabular.ipynb, which trains one MLP on the single shipped Electricity file. Nothing in the repository trains the tabular ResNet, builds the 10-dataset benchmark, aggregates per-dataset curves with 95% CIs, or computes the table entries of Table 1 / Figure 2 / Figure 4.
findings.concern: Every tabular number in the paper (4 datasets x MLP/ResNet x 3 methods, the 10-dataset Figure 2, the Figure 4 retraining curves) is unreproducible; the paper's cross-dataset claim has no producing code.
findings.resolution: Release the experiment drivers for Table 1, Figure 2 and Figure 4 (splits, MLP/ResNet definitions, CE_KL computation, 10-dataset aggregation and CI bootstrap), with the datasets or a fetch script, or state explicitly that the released repository is only a demo.
findings.sourcePaper: Improving Perturbation-based Explanations by Understanding the Role of Uncertainty Calibration

findings.title: Bias is measured against an in-sample AIPW estimate, not the known true ATE
findings.claim: The '|bias|' reported for every estimator in Table 3 is |τ̂_S − τ̂aipw|, where τ̂aipw is computed from the same RCT rows of the same single dataset (aipw_borrow returns it as tau_exp).  The true ATE is never used, although the DGP is released and makes it exactly computable: with simulate_data.py's seeds (random_state=42) the sample ATEs of the shipped rct_data_linear_0.1.csv and rct_data_exp_0.1.csv are 0.34991 and 5.37718 (_audit_code/check_true_ate.py).
findings.concern: Against the true ATE, at Linear Top-K=10 the AIPW benchmark (τ̂=0.28551, error 0.0644) is *closer* to the truth than τ̂if (0.28492, error 0.0650), while Table 3 reports τ̂if as 13× better than τ̂lasso (0.0006 vs 0.0082) when the true errors are 0.0650 vs 0.0726; in the Nonlinear arm the benchmark itself is 3.95 away from the truth (73 % of the ATE), so the reported |bias| ≈ 0.018 cannot detect that all estimators are grossly wrong.  The same functional, (τ̂_S − τ̂aipw)² + Var(ψ)/n, is what §6.2 uses to select K, so the column offered as evidence of accuracy is also the method's own selection criterion.
findings.resolution: Report bias against the true ATE implied by the simulation DGP (per replicate, and against the sample ATE) alongside the current column, and re-state the §8.2 conclusions on that basis.
findings.sourcePaper: Adaptive Data-Borrowing for Improving Treatment Effect Estimation using External Controls

findings.title: Reasoning Gym test set (96 x 100) is the 9600-sample validation set
findings.quote: 0,test prompts implied by '100 samples from each reasoning gym task' x 96 tasks,9600,9600,IDENTICAL,equals the '9600 validation samples' of Appendix E.4 exactly
findings.claim: Sec. 3.4 says 'For logic puzzles, we reserved 100 samples from each reasoning gym tasks as test datasets for evaluation' (p. 5) and Appendix E.4 says 'we generate a large dataset consisting of 37K synthetic training samples and 9600 validation samples, spanning 96 tasks' (p. 26). 96 tasks x 100 = 9600 exactly, and Table 4 accounts for only 37k Reasoning Gym samples in total, so the most consistent reading of the paper is that the set it calls validation is the same set it calls test (the paper never describes a third, separate 9600-prompt set); Appendix F further confirms the training-time monitoring set contains 'the logic puzzle graph_color from Reasoning Gym'.
findings.concern: The headline logic-puzzle result (base 4.24 -> ours 59.06, i.e. the +54.8% quoted in the Introduction) is measured on the same prompts that were monitored during training and that triggered reference-policy/optimizer resets, so it is not a held-out estimate.
findings.resolution: Authors: state explicitly whether the 9600 validation samples and the 96 x 100 test samples are disjoint, give the seeds/ranges used to generate each, and report the Reasoning Gym scores on a held-out split that was never used for monitoring. Note that Reasoning Gym datasets are generated deterministically from (dataset, seed, index) (reasoning_gym/dataset.py:13-20), so overlap is guaranteed if the same seed range is reused.
findings.sourcePaper: ProRL: Prolonged Reinforcement Learning Expands Reasoning Boundaries in Large Language Models

findings.title: Cosine path allocates 125 GiB of host RAM for the shipped config and crashes when `dataset_size` is left at its default
findings.quote:
a1 = torch.empty(
        (dataset_size * max_length, model.config.hidden_size),
        dtype=torch.bfloat16,
        device='cpu'
    )
    a2 = torch.empty(
        (dataset_size * max_length, model.config.hidden_size),
        dtype=torch.bfloat16,
        device='cpu'
    )
findings.claim: Both activation buffers are sized `dataset_size * max_length` rows times the hidden size, regardless of how many tokens are actually produced. With the shipped reproduction config (`dataset_size: 8000`, `max_length: 1024`) and Llama-3-8B's 4096 hidden units this is 8 192 000 × 4096 × 2 B = 62.5 GiB per buffer, 125 GiB for a1+a2 (`_audit_code/check_cosine_memory.py`, `out/check_cosine_memory.csv`). `dataset_size` is `Optional[int] = None` by default, and `None * max_length` raises `TypeError`.
findings.concern: Reproducing the paper's best-performing (Cosine) variant therefore requires >125 GiB of host RAM and silently fails with a `TypeError` if the documented optional argument is omitted, so the headline variant is effectively not runnable on ordinary hardware.
findings.resolution: Please size the buffers from the number of tokens actually collected (or accumulate the Gram matrix as `lstsq` does), and make `dataset_size` required or default it to the full dataset.
findings.sourcePaper: ReplaceMe: Network Simplification via Depth Pruning and Transformer Block Linearization

findings.title: Released optimiser is AdamW lr=1e-3; paper states Adam l=1e-4
findings.claim: The RoPE offsets are optimised with torch.optim.AdamW(..., lr=1e-3), and the CLI exposes neither a learning-rate nor an optimiser flag. §A.3 (p. 22) states 'We utilize Adam optimizer across all methods' and '5. Ours: l = 1 × 10−4, s = 5, t = 10' (check_hyperparams.py).
findings.concern: The released code optimises with a 10x larger learning rate and with AdamW weight decay rather than Adam, so the paper's stated hyper-parameters do not reproduce the released behaviour and the reported numbers cannot be traced to a documented setting.
findings.resolution: Report which learning rate and optimiser produced Tables 1-3, expose them as CLI flags, and align code, §A.3 and the README.
findings.paperRef: §A.3, p. 22 ('5. Ours: l = 1 × 10−4, s = 5, t = 10'; 'We utilize Adam optimizer across all methods')
findings.sourcePaper: RoPECraft: Training-Free Motion Transfer with Trajectory-Guided RoPE Optimization on Diffusion Transformers

findings.title: Table 1 counts half the Hamming distance of the ranking permutation, not class-ranking inversions
findings.claim:
The per-update "class ranking change" is the number of positions at which the argsort
permutation of the class probabilities differs from the previous one, divided by two (the
in-code comment reads "we always need to divide by 2 otherwise one change will be counted
twice"). The paper defines the same quantity as "counting pairwise inversions in class
rankings before and after each exploration update" (Table 1 caption, p. 9).
findings.concern:
Half the Hamming distance of a permutation is not its inversion count: for the 276 pairs of
rankings of 4 classes the two quantities disagree in 228 cases (83 %), e.g. a rotation
(0,1,2,3)->(1,2,3,0) gives 2 instead of 3, and a cyclic shift of n classes gives n//2 instead
of n-1 (`_audit_code/check_rank_change_metric.py`). Every Table 1 entry is therefore a
systematically under-counted version of the quantity the paper describes, and the counts are
additionally taken only on the 101 saved snapshots (save_each = 10), so inversions that occur
and revert between snapshots are invisible.
findings.resolution:
Recompute Table 1 with a true inversion count (e.g. Kendall tau between consecutive
probability vectors) on the saved snapshots, and state that changes are observed only every
10 iterations.
findings.paperRef: Table 1 caption, p. 9 ('counting pairwise inversions in class rankings ...')
findings.sourcePaper: Unveiling Transformer Perception by Exploring Input Manifolds

findings.title: Paper reports Welch t-tests with all p<1e-3; code runs a one-sample t-test and returns p=0.007
findings.quote:
"# p-values of Welch t-tests on the ratios of the volumes explored by SIMExp over those explored by SIMEC\n",
    "# Always rejecting the null hypothesis, i.e. that the ratio is <= 1, i.e. that SIMEC explored more than SIMExp\n",
    "volume_ratios.groupby([\"dataset_name\", \"delta_multiplier\"]).agg(\n",
    "    volume_ratio_test=(\"svd_volume_ratio\", lambda x: ttest_1samp(x, popmean = 1, alternative = \"greater\").statistic),\n",
    "    #avg_norm = (\"avg_norm\", np.mean),\n",
    "    volume_ratio_test_pvalue=(\"svd_volume_ratio\", lambda x: ttest_1samp(x, popmean = 1, alternative = \"greater\").pvalue)\n",
findings.claim:
The reported validation of the hyper-volume ratio ρV is a *one-sample* t-test of the
per-patch ratios against popmean = 1 (alternative "greater"), despite the comment (and the
paper) calling it a Welch t-test; the p-values it produced are stored in
tables/volume_ratio.csv, whose row 5 is
`hatespeech,10.0,2.44,0.007`.
findings.concern:
Two problems in one place: (i) the test named in the paper ("Welch t-tests on ρV", p. 8) is
not the test that was run, and the ratios are in fact paired per (input, repetition) so a
paired/blocked test (or a mixed model accounting for patches nested in inputs) is the
appropriate one; (ii) the paper states "all p-values resulted lower than 1e-3", which is
contradicted by the repository's own output, where MHS with η = 10 gives p = 0.007.
findings.resolution:
Report the test actually used with its assumptions (one-sample vs paired vs two-sample),
correct the "all p-values < 1e-3" sentence (7 of 8 are < 1e-3, one is 0.007), and account for
the nesting of patches within inputs.
findings.paperRef: Section 4, p. 8 ('We validated these results by performing Welch t-tests on ρV : all p-values resulted lower than 10−3')
findings.sourcePaper: Unveiling Transformer Perception by Exploring Input Manifolds

findings.title: Normalisation mean/std fitted on 2017-2024, including the 2024 test year
findings.claim: The z-score statistics used by MIGN (dataset/dataset.py:46) and by the baselines (dataset/dataset.py:250-251) are np.nanmean/np.nanstd over a matrix built from *every* per-day CSV in <base_path>/<variable>, and step0_filter_feature.py:23 writes those CSVs for years 2017..2024. Nothing restricts the fit to the 2017-2022 training years.
findings.concern: Preprocessing is fitted on the full period, so the training-time scaling depends on the 2023 validation and 2024 test distributions; the effect on the reported MSE/MAE is small because it is a single global affine rescaling, but the released pipeline is not train-only preprocessing.
findings.resolution: Recompute climatology on 2017-2022 only (or confirm the released climatology.npy was produced that way) and state which period was used in Section 4.
findings.sourcePaper: Mesh Interpolation Graph Network for Dynamic and Spatially Irregular Global Weather Forecasting

findings.title: No code for the H-ensemble / MCW / MADA / WADN rows of Table 2
findings.quote: - **otherpoint_list**: Specifies additional evaluation points; currently supports `m` ,`all` and `none`, which are stand for `OTQMS`,`'Allsources+Target`and`Target-Only`.
findings.claim: The released driver can only run OTQMS, AllSources+Target and Target-Only; grep over the repository finds no reference to H-ensemble, MCW, MADA or WADN (0 hits), and no other training entry point exists.
findings.concern: Appendix D.4 states that MCW, H-ensemble, MADA and WADN were re-run by the authors under the paper's setting, but their Table 2 numbers (e.g. WADN 50.5 / 58.7 average) cannot be reproduced or audited, so five of the nine rows that the 'significant improvement over state-of-the-art' claim rests on are unverifiable.
findings.resolution: Release the adapted baseline training/evaluation code (or the configs and scripts) for MCW, H-ensemble, MADA and WADN, since Appendix D.4 says they were run in-house.

findings.title: Default config stores algo as the string 'both', the drivers test for the list ['both']
findings.claim: `prepare_experiment.py --default` writes `"algo": "both"` (prepare_experiment.py:591, a str; the interactive path likewise returns a str when a single choice is typed). Compared with the list literal `["both"]` the branch can never fire, so the driver silently runs SiMEC only (the check script evaluates the real branch and gets `algorithms = ['simec']`). `experiments/bert_exploration.py:159-163` has the identical test, and `experiments/group_results.py:167` (`... if p["algo"] == ["both"] else p["algo"]`) then iterates over the characters ['b','o','t','h'] instead of the two algorithms; the `f"{algorithm}-" in f` filter then matches directories for accidental reasons (the check script reproduces this: 'mnist-...' matches 't-', 'hatespeech-...' matches 'h-', 'target-word' matches 't-'), so the collected rows are stored under algorithm labels 't'/'h' which no downstream analysis selects.
findings.concern: With the released default configuration the pipeline never produces a single SiMExp run and then collects nothing, although all SiMExp results (blue curves of Fig. 2a, the four SiMExp rows of Table 1, every volume ratio) come from those runs.
findings.resolution: Please confirm how `algo` was actually set for the reported runs and fix the three call sites to accept the string form (`params["algo"] in ("both", ["both"])`). analysis/generate_results_df.py:157-159 already handles the string form correctly, which suggests the string is the intended value.
findings.sourcePaper: Unveiling Transformer Perception by Exploring Input Manifolds

findings.title: PRR counts a refuse-indicative string anywhere in the answer, not a response prefix
findings.claim: The released matcher tests substring containment of any of the 31 prefixes anywhere in the whole response. Appendix B.1.1 Eq. (7) defines PRR as 1(exists p in P, Prefix(y_i) = p), i.e. equality of the response's leading segment. On a hand-built fixture of two real refusals and five compliant answers, the released predicate returns 0.857 while Eq. (7) returns 0.286 (out/check_prr_prefix.csv; run check_prr_prefix.py).
findings.concern: Compliant answers that merely contain "illegal", "unethical", "I cannot" or "I must" are counted as refusals, which inflates PRR - the primary metric of Tables 1, 3, 8 and 9. Under the Appendix B.5 system prompt the model is told to begin "Sorry, I can't help with that.", so an answer that opens with the mandated phrase and then complies is also counted as a refusal.
findings.resolution: Align the implementation with Eq. (7) (startswith, or a documented judge), re-run the PRR columns, and report the effect on the 85.34%/29.85% claims.
findings.paperRef: Appendix B.1.1 Eq. (7) (p. 19); Section 4 Metrics (p. 7); Appendix B.5 (p. 24)
findings.sourcePaper: EVOREFUSE: Evolutionary Prompt Optimization for Evaluation and Mitigation of LLM Over-Refusal to Pseudo-Malicious Instructions

findings.title: Step size takes the min over ALL eigenvalues, so delta is fixed by the 1e-6 epsilon
findings.quote:
abs_eigenvalues = torch.abs(eigenvalues)
            root_max_lambda = torch.sqrt(abs_eigenvalues.max(dim = -1, keepdims = True)[0] / (abs_eigenvalues.min(dim = -1, keepdims = True)[0] + eps))
            root_max_lambda = root_max_lambda[:batch_size, :max_len, 0]
            # root_max_lambda.shape = (batch_size, len(eq_class_emb_ids))
            delta = delta_multiplier * torch.ones_like(root_max_lambda) / root_max_lambda
findings.claim: delta = delta_multiplier / sqrt(max|lambda| / (min|lambda| + eps)) with eps = 1e-6 (line 266), and the minimum is taken over all |lambda|, including the near-zero ones: the per-patch pullback has rank at most the number of retained logits (10) in an embedding space of 384 (ViT) or 768 (BERT). The paper defines delta(k) = eta * sqrt(min_{j:lambda_j != 0}|lambda_j| / max_j|lambda_j|), i.e. the inverse square root of the condition number over non-zero eigenvalues. _audit_code/check_delta_formula.py reproduces the implemented delta to 10 digits as eta*sqrt(1e-6/lambda_max), four orders of magnitude below the paper's value for a random but full-rank per-patch Jacobian.
findings.concern: The step-size rule that the paper justifies theoretically is not the implemented one: the effective step is set by an arbitrary epsilon constant rather than by the spectrum, and it is the same for SiMEC and SiMExp.
findings.resolution: Either implement the printed rule (exclude zero eigenvalues) and re-run, or state the rule actually used, delta = eta*sqrt(eps/lambda_max), and justify it.
findings.paperRef: Section 3.1 paragraph 'There are some remarks to point out...'; Algorithm 1 line 7
findings.sourcePaper: Unveiling Transformer Perception by Exploring Input Manifolds

findings.claim: The model registry contains only OLinear variants; there is no model class for iTransformer, PatchTST, RLinear, Leddam, Fredformer or Timer anywhere in the repo, and no driver script passes the --iTrans_linear / --PatchTST_linear / --Leddam_attnLinear / --iTrans_ortho_trans / --PatchTST_ortho_trans / --DLinear_ortho_trans flags that run.py declares for them (checked over all 123 scripts).
findings.concern: Table 5 (OrthoTrans applied to iTransformer/PatchTST/RLinear), Table 9 (NormLin applied to iTransformer/PatchTST/Leddam/Fredformer) and Table 10 (NormLin inside the pretrained Timer, fine-tuned and zero-shot) are the evidence for the abstract's claim that the module 'consistently enhances Transformer-based forecasters', and none of them can be produced or checked from the release.
findings.resolution: Release the modified forecaster files (iTransformer/PatchTST/RLinear/Leddam/Fredformer with the OrthoTrans and NormLin switches), the Timer fine-tuning/zero-shot code and UTSD checkpoint recipe, and the driver scripts/commands that generate Tables 5, 9 and 10.

findings.title: COVID-19 S2 fits its fixed transform on 70% of the series while training uses only 60%
findings.claim: The S2 driver uses --data custom2, i.e. a 6:2:2 split (Dataset_Custom2, data_provider/data_loader.py:430-431), but still loads Q matrices computed from the first 70% of the 335-row series; the matrices are reproduced exactly by the released recipe at ratio 0.7 (_audit_code/out/check_qmat_all.csv), so rows 201-233 (about 10% of the series and roughly the first half of the validation block, rows 201-267) contribute to the fixed transform.
findings.concern: A fixed preprocessing artefact that the paper describes as computed on the training set is in fact fitted partly on validation data for COVID-19 S2 (the test block, rows 268-335, is untouched, so the test metric itself is not compromised).
findings.resolution: Regenerate the COVID Q matrices with train_ratio=0.6 (as was done for unemployment, which correctly uses *_ratio0.6.npy) and confirm which ratio produced the Table 3 COVID row.
findings.paperRef: Table 11 (p.26) reports COVID-19 S2 as 6:2:2; Section 4.2 defines CorrMat_t from X_train
findings.sourcePaper: OLinear: A Linear Model for Time Series Forecasting in Orthogonally Transformed Domain
